Pocket Kingdom, developed by 08 Games and published by Plug In Digital and WhisperGames, is an indie puzzle-platformer that embraces a nostalgic, retro approach to design while building its own peculiar and imaginative identity. The game begins with a humorous yet intriguing premise: a financially troubled photographer is hired to document a sleeping god located somewhere in a fragmented, floating island kingdom suspended among the clouds. What follows is a journey through interconnected environments filled with mechanical contraptions, eccentric inhabitants, and a rich assortment of physics-based challenges. Although simple on the surface, the world feels layered and inviting, presenting players with a blend of exploration, puzzle solving, and mechanical experimentation that encourages deep engagement with its systems.

The visual style of Pocket Kingdom leans heavily into a pixel-art aesthetic reminiscent of Amiga-era games, with a steampunk influence shaping the appearance of machinery, devices, and architectural elements scattered throughout the island. The artwork may appear rough around the edges compared to modern pixel-art standards, but the charm lies in how intentionally handcrafted everything feels. Backgrounds, characters, and objects carry a distinct personality that reinforces the quirky tone of the narrative. Complementing the visuals is an upbeat chiptune soundtrack that underscores the sense of adventure, though its limited variety means the music loops often and may fatigue players during long sessions. Nonetheless, the pairing of sights and sounds builds an atmosphere that feels both nostalgic and whimsical, anchoring the game’s identity firmly in the indie puzzle tradition.

Gameplay is where Pocket Kingdom truly distinguishes itself. Rather than relying on traditional platforming techniques or fast reflexes, the game emphasizes experimentation with tools, environmental manipulation, and altered physics. Gravity-switching boots, grapple hooks, rockets, and movable blocks all play a role in navigating self-contained puzzle rooms, each of which introduces new mechanics or challenges designed to stretch the player’s understanding of the world. Many puzzles are built around clever twists such as teleportation loops, screen wrapping, or interacting with multiple objects in sequence to create a chain reaction. The gradual layering of these concepts results in a puzzle structure that rewards curiosity and observation, and while some challenges initially appear opaque, the solutions often feel satisfying once fully understood.

The narrative thread woven through Pocket Kingdom adds a gentle sense of direction without overshadowing the gameplay. NPCs provide cryptic hints, fragments of world lore, and occasional humor, helping the player piece together the rules of the island while adding personality to the floating kingdom’s eccentric residents. The progression structure encourages both backtracking and organic discovery, as new tools often unlock previously inaccessible sections of older rooms. This design helps the player form a mental map of the world, turning the experience into a layered exploration where each area folds back into others in subtle, interconnected ways. Even though the plot itself is not deeply developed, the storytelling complements the puzzles and reinforces the game’s dreamlike, slightly surreal tone.

Pocket Kingdom has been met with consistently positive feedback from players who appreciate its inventive mechanics, creative puzzle design, and distinctive atmosphere. Many highlight the cleverness of its challenges, the charm of its handmade pixel world, and the sense of discovery that comes from learning how its many systems interlock. While the total playtime is not extensive, the density of ideas and the complexity embedded in individual puzzles give the experience a sense of depth that feels proportional to its size. For those who enjoy methodical puzzle solving, intricate environmental mechanics, and a world that gradually reveals itself through experimentation, Pocket Kingdom offers a refreshing and memorable adventure.

However, the game is not without its drawbacks. Some puzzles rely on mechanics that can feel unintuitive at first, occasionally leading to moments of frustration where the solution seems unclear. Visual clarity can sometimes suffer due to the game’s retro art style, making certain interactive objects blend into the environment. The soundtrack, while charming, may begin to feel repetitive. Yet these shortcomings tend to diminish in importance when balanced against the creativity and personality of the overall experience. Pocket Kingdom remains a standout example of a tightly crafted indie puzzle-platformer—compact, inventive, and undeniably charming.

In the end, Pocket Kingdom succeeds as a thoughtful and imaginative journey through a quirky, floating world filled with secrets and surprises. Its puzzle design, narrative whimsy, and retro-inspired presentation combine to create a game that feels timeless in its simplicity yet rich in its execution. For players who appreciate puzzlers that rely on observation, experimentation, and a touch of surreal humor, Pocket Kingdom delivers a rewarding and quietly enchanting experience from start to finish.

Иммунны к этой странной магии только переходы между комнатами — лестницы и двери. Заколдовало карманное королевство таинственное божество, которое точно так же сидит где-то здесь вместе со всеми.

Когда карта локаций становится достаточно обширной, игра выдает тебе свободный телепорт — который, как и всё здесь, тоже иногда используется в головоломках. 

В целом мне до такой степени понравилось, что я после финала решил ещё раз всё оббегать, поискать оставшиеся секреты — чего я почти никогда не делаю в играх, тем более пазлах. [code] [quote=Wendrex] 1. Concept and Creative Vision

Pocket Kingdom is an indie adventure developed by 08 Games, released in December 2016. Blending steampunk aesthetics with detailed pixel art and an immersive chiptune soundtrack, the game serves as a heartfelt homage to classic Amiga-era titles, while also introducing modern twists that make it feel fresh and unique.

2. Setting and Mysterious Narrative

You play as a struggling photographer sent to capture images of a mysterious god on a floating, magic-infused island. Upon arrival, you find yourself stranded—setting the stage for an enigmatic journey through charming environments and quirky characters, each with their own curious stories.

3. Visuals and Soundtrack

The visual style is one of the game’s strongest assets: polished pixel art with a steampunk flavor that feels both nostalgic and original. The chiptune soundtrack enhances immersion, adding rhythm and personality to the world.

4. Gameplay and Puzzle Mechanics

Although Pocket Kingdom is a platformer at heart, it avoids genre clichés. There’s no jumping—instead, you climb blocks and use special gear like gravity boots, rocket launchers, and grappling devices. The puzzles rely on physics, positioning, and logic, making each room a unique challenge.
The world is non-linear, filled with secrets and alternate paths that reward exploration and curiosity. The average playtime is around 4 hours, offering solid content for a low price.

5. Reception and Player Feedback

On Steam, the game holds a “Very Positive” rating, with around 89–91% approval across 100–200 reviews.
Critics and players alike praise the originality, style, and puzzle mechanics. However, a few areas show room for improvement:

The story is more atmospheric than deep—great for setting the tone, but lacking in major narrative arcs or emotional stakes.

Some puzzle rooms contain unnecessary elements that can mislead players and cause overthinking.

6. Strengths

Striking visual style: pixel art full of charm and personality.

Inventive mechanics: gravity manipulation, laser gadgets, rocket tools, and more.

Unique atmosphere: a floating world that begs to be explored.

Great value: compact but rich gameplay for an affordable price.

7. Areas for Growth

Expanding the story—adding a clearer arc or stronger emotional motivation could enhance the experience.

Fine-tuning puzzle design to ensure each element serves a purpose (or hiding red herrings better if intentional).

Final Thoughts

Pocket Kingdom is a pixelated gem—a game that honors its retro inspirations with care and style, while also standing out with original mechanics and a whimsical floating world. Pocket Kingdom is a mobile app that's been dumped on Steam as if it was a real PC game (it's not)... it's a cash grab from greedy mobile devs.  This mobile app is yet another of literally thousands of 2D retro platformers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere.

There's some heavy puzzle elements to this platformer, which might work well if they were paired with high quality delivery (even Hollow Knight did well despite the 2D graphics), but the delivery here is garbage tier, invalidating any other elements of the game completely. But what else should we expect from mobile apps being dumped on Steam like this?

From a technical perspective, as a mobile app, this doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The controls and game handling are notably very clunky and unsmooth here.  It's janky and unsatisfying to play... and any experienced gamer will tell you, the handling, responsiveness and general gameplay feel of the control scheme must be well polished for this kind of game to succeed.  Unfortunately, this is something the developer seems to have phoned in, with little to no apparent gameplay testing.  They dropped the ball on this one.

Because this is a mobile app, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the iPhones that the mobile app was designed for.  These are unfortunate handicaps and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was an afterthought for the iPhone developers who are to blame for this.  The mobile app is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for mobile phones forces upon a game.  Once more, mobile devs have made gaming worse for everyone.  I didn't spend thousands on building a gaming rig just so I could pretend it's an iPhone.

These technical defects push this mobile app below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Pocket Kingdom didn't appeal much to the people who own a copy of the mobile app, either.  It has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the mobile app didn't really capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for encountering a laser, one of the first things you do in the game, trivial to get, but less than 30 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the mobile app.  Hardly a success story, even the people who own this mobile app weren't interested in it.

Reviewing SteamDB to check how popular this mobile app was with players reveals a surprise... there's a modest spike in player counts for the mobile app.  But this only happened once, around the same time that trading cards were applied to the mobile app... so this is just card idlers getting their cards and moving on.  A closer look at the numbers shows the mobile app just has a couple of players every week running up the mobile app and idling it for cards, then deleting it.  We must ask how it benefits gamers for there to be so many mobile apps like this, with no merit as a serious game, that only generate sales from people idling and selling the trading cards.

So, should you buy this mobile app?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Once more we see greedy mobile devs trying to scam PC gamers. On Steam, this is $7 USD, on app stores, it's $3.50. Mobile devs must learn PC gamers are not here to be gouged, and can't be expected to pay TWICE THE PRICE for an already overpriced mobile app just because it's been lazily dumped on Steam.  This is unacceptable disrespect for PC gamers.  Because this is a mobile app, is priced to insult and gouge PC gamers, and because of the other defects, it's impossible to recommend.

Truly an Indie Gem. Puzzles are well-designed. You really have to think out of the box as the laws of physics work in particular ways in the Pocket Kingdom. There are simple gadgets in the game (gun to push objects and grappler to pull) and remarkably, if a puzzle can be solved without gadgets, then bringing those tools from another level doesn't really help you. So, no sneaky "cheating". Really well thought out level design. 
It also feels like you found a little gem because the community around it is so small. Like it is everyone's little secret. And if you're stuck, there are no easy walkthroughs to come by, so gotta use your brain.

It has promise, but Pocket Kingdom is clunky, unintuitive and lacks some serious QOL features. The map is hard to read, the game has tons of strobing laser lights you can't turn off that hurt your eyes if you sit in the dark and the gameplay itself is a bit too simple to be fun. The pixel art is pretty at first, but it makes puzzles very hard to read and take in, so you kind of just do random things until something happens - most of the puzzles consist of moving or shooting boxes as well as ziplining (but never both at the same time, as you can only carry one tool).

Because of how hard to read the puzzles are at first glance, this trial & error gets frustrating very quickly. Many of the tiles also look somewhat similar and - the worst part - almost every room has switches that do *something*, but you don't know what until you activate it, further exacerbating that trial & error. There are also a ton of weird features that are not fully explained - for example. you eventually unlock fast travel to previously visited / solved rooms, but the game does not communicate that to you clearly at all, and the same goes for some other features.

After a few hours, the game just drags on and I could not bring myself to finish it. The concept of a metroidvania-ish puzzle is cool, but the execution is sorely lacking thanks to the confusing navigation, puzzle presentation and hard-on-the-eyes visual style. I would recommend against it.
It's a fairly challenging puzzle game with a neat aesthetic, if it's on sale or in a bundle I'd recommend scooping it up for a good day or two of fun and mild frustration haha

A fairly good Metroidvania-y puzzle platformer. Doesn't really break the mold as far as this particular flavour of puzzle game goes (wraparound edges), but it does introduce enough content throughout to keep things fresh. While puzzles aren't as tightly knit as for it not to occasionally feel like you stumbled into a solution rather than having thought it through, many of the times you are limited you do feel like it was your fault for missing/forgetting something obvious. And sometimes the lateral thinking involved did feel awesome, which is always a welcome thing.

Story (there's a bit of it, though most of the lore is gotten through conversation with the statically placed characters throughout the map) does end somewhat anticlimatically. Unlocking the ending basically requires two things which are received independently, but there's a distinct feeling of "wait, that was it?" when you get there. The cutscene does feature a minor teaser and I didn't explore all rooms, so maybe a better ending hiding somewhere.
